Part 1 Objectives

  1. List and describe common pulmonary congenital anomalies
  2. Describe atelectasis; discuss types of atelectasis and their etiologies, mechanism, and pathologic findings
  3. Describe pulmonary edema and list cardiogenic causes
  4. List causes of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), describe the mechanism of formation, and describe the clinical presentation and pathologic changes
PART 1 — Congenital Anomalies, Atelectasis, Edema & ARDS

1. Congenital Anomalies

Pulmonary hypoplasiaThe organ fails to reach its normal size during development — distinct from atrophy, where an organ reaches normal size and then shrinks
Foregut cystsBronchogenic, esophageal, or enteric — a cyst is simply a space lined by epithelium, and the epithelial type tells you the origin: respiratory-type epithelium (bronchogenic), squamous epithelium (esophageal), or GI-type epithelium (enteric)
Pulmonary sequestrationExtralobar or intralobar; pulmonary tissue that is anatomically separate ("sequestered") from the rest of the normal lung. It must have a connection to the aorta (or its branches) to receive blood supply, but has no connection to the airway.
Complications differ by type — Extralobar sequestration is usually asymptomatic and found/removed incidentally. Intralobar sequestration can lead to pneumonia and bronchiectasis: even though there's no airway connection, the sequestered tissue still has a blood supply, and transient bacteremia (which is common — e.g., after dental procedures) can seed that isolated tissue with infection that has no way to clear normally, since it lacks a connecting airway.
Extralobar pulmonary sequestration
A small, separate nodule of essentially normal-appearing pulmonary parenchyma, with a probe demonstrating its distinct vascular connection — separate from the main bronchial tree and the rest of the lung's normal blood supply.

Left vs. Right Lung — A Trick Worth Knowing

Most people answer this by counting lobes (3 on the right, 2 on the left) — and that usually works. But it's not foolproof: a partial fissure can make a 2-lobed lung look like it has a third lobe. The anatomically reliable distinguishing feature is actually the relationship between the pulmonary artery and the bronchus: on the left, the pulmonary artery sits above the bronchus; on the right, the pulmonary artery sits in front of (anterior to) the bronchus. This relationship holds consistently across all lungs.

Left lung — the trick case
This lung shows a partial cleft about two-thirds of the way down, which can make it look like it has three lobes at first glance — but it only has two. Counting lobes alone would lead to the wrong answer here.
Right lung — three true lobes
Clear, complete fissures separating three distinct lobes — the normal right lung anatomy.

Bronchogenic Cyst — Example

Bronchogenic cyst — low power
A cystic space lined by a fibrous wall — the low-power overview before assessing the epithelial lining.
Bronchogenic cyst — high power
At higher power, tall, pseudostratified columnar (respiratory-type) epithelium with visible cilia lines the cyst — identifying it as bronchogenic rather than esophageal (squamous) or enteric (GI-type). The epithelium appears somewhat degraded here from postmortem autolysis, which can make identification trickier, but the ciliated columnar character is still visible.

USMLE-Style Question

A newborn is found to have a mass of pulmonary tissue below the left lower lobe that receives its blood supply directly from the descending aorta but has no connection to the tracheobronchial tree. Several weeks later, the infant develops fever and is found to have pneumonia isolated to this mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Extralobar pulmonary sequestration
B. Intralobar pulmonary sequestration
C. Bronchogenic cyst
D. Pulmonary hypoplasia
E. Congenital lobar emphysema
Answer: B. Intralobar sequestration is the form associated with pneumonia and bronchiectasis, because the sequestered tissue has a blood supply (allowing bacteremic seeding) but no airway connection (preventing normal clearance of infection). Extralobar sequestration is usually asymptomatic and found incidentally.

2. Atelectasis

Description: collapse of the airspaces. Three types, distinguished by mechanism and the direction of resulting mediastinal shift.

TypeMechanismSpecific Etiologies
ResorptiveAirway blockage — air distal to the obstruction is absorbed into the bloodstream, but the airspace cannot refillTumor in the airway; mucous plug; foreign body in the airway
CompressiveFluid (or air) in the pleural space compresses the lung, preventing the airspaces from fillingPneumothorax (air in pleural cavity); hemothorax (blood in pleural cavity); pleural effusion
ContractionScarring of the lung impairs filling of the airspaces, which collapseInterstitial lung disease
Reasoning through the mechanism — Resorptive atelectasis: air trapped distal to a blockage gets absorbed into the blood over time with nothing replacing it, so that segment collapses. Compressive atelectasis: something external (fluid, air) is physically pushing against the lung, working against the pressure needed to keep the airspace open. Contraction atelectasis: scarring itself prevents the space from ever filling properly in the first place.
Compressive atelectasis with pleural adhesion
This patient had bilateral pneumothorax causing compression of the airspaces. The visible fibrous band is an adhesion between the lung and the inner chest wall surface — a reminder that these processes can leave lasting structural connections behind.
Complete atelectasis — heart and both lungs at autopsy
Normally, autopsy lungs are filled with air and will visibly "stand up" on the table. Here, both lungs are completely flat — a striking demonstration of the volume loss atelectasis produces.
Atelectasis vs. normal lung — direct histologic comparison
One field capturing both patterns at once: open, air-filled alveolar spaces on one side contrast sharply with densely collapsed, airless tissue on the other — no distinguishable alveolar spaces are visible in the atelectatic portion at all.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient develops a large pleural effusion that progressively compresses the adjacent lung over several days. Which of the following best describes the expected pathologic finding?

A. Irreversible collapse due to loss of elastic recoil
B. Collapse of airspaces due to external compression, potentially reversible once the effusion is drained
C. Collapse due to airway obstruction from a mucous plug
D. Collapse due to interstitial fibrosis
E. No collapse would be expected from a pleural effusion
Answer: B. This describes compressive atelectasis — external fluid in the pleural space compresses the lung and prevents the airspaces from filling; unlike contraction atelectasis (from fibrosis), this type is typically reversible once the underlying fluid/air is removed.

3. Pulmonary Edema

Description: fluid in the airspaces and/or the pleural cavities. Forms: cardiogenic (i.e., hemodynamic) and non-cardiogenic. Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema is essentially synonymous with ARDS (Section 4) — so when the term "pulmonary edema" is used without qualification, it typically refers to the cardiogenic/hemodynamic form.

Why "hemodynamic" is a better term than "cardiogenic" — Several causes of hemodynamic edema have nothing to do with the heart itself (e.g., hypoalbuminemia from liver disease or nephrotic syndrome), so "hemodynamic" more accurately captures the shared mechanism: a disturbance of the Starling forces governing fluid movement across capillary walls.
CategoryCauses
↑ Hydrostatic pressureLeft-sided heart failure (blood backs up into the lungs, raising vascular pressure); volume overload; pulmonary vein obstruction (impairs venous return from the lungs)
↓ Oncotic pressureHypoalbuminemia (albumin normally draws fluid back into vessels from the interstitium); nephrotic syndrome (kidney loses albumin); liver disease (albumin is synthesized in the liver); protein-losing enteropathy
Pulmonary edema — pleural effusion
Watery fluid filling the pleural cavity at autopsy — one of the two places pulmonary edema fluid can be found (the other being within the alveolar airspaces themselves).
Pulmonary edema — alveolar fluid, histology
Alveolar airspaces filled with homogeneous (uniform), pale eosinophilic (light pink), essentially acellular fluid — occasional alveolar macrophages may be present, but there is no true inflammatory infiltrate. This bland, uniform appearance is the key histologic signature distinguishing simple edema fluid from an infectious/inflammatory process.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with cirrhosis and severe hypoalbuminemia develops bilateral pulmonary edema. Which mechanism best explains this finding?

A. Decreased oncotic pressure, impairing fluid return to the vasculature
B. Increased hydrostatic pressure from left heart failure
C. Direct alveolar epithelial injury with hyaline membrane formation
D. Pulmonary vein obstruction
E. Increased capillary permeability from sepsis
Answer: A. Liver disease causes decreased albumin synthesis, lowering plasma oncotic pressure. Since albumin is what normally draws fluid back into the vasculature from the interstitium, low oncotic pressure allows fluid to accumulate in the lungs (and elsewhere) — a hemodynamic mechanism unrelated to the heart itself.

4. Acute Lung Injury / ARDS

Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) — formerly "adult respiratory distress syndrome," renamed once it became clear children can develop the same process — is essentially non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

Clinical Features

  • Abrupt onset of hypoxemia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates
  • Does not respond well to ventilatory support — and mechanical ventilation can itself sometimes contribute to worsening the process

Pathogenesis

Anything that damages the alveolar-capillary membrane — which is essentially just an epithelium and an endothelium with little else between them — allows protein-rich fluid from inside the vessel to leak out onto the alveolar septum.

  1. Endothelial (or epithelial) injury — e.g., sepsis (damages endothelium from within the blood), or direct epithelial injury (e.g., inhaled toxic gas)
  2. Endothelial activation → release of adhesion molecules, pro-coagulant factors, cytokines
  3. Neutrophil adhesion — the single most important cell type in this process — releasing proteases and reactive oxygen species, amplifying tissue damage
  4. Accumulation of intra-alveolar protein-rich fluid (this is why it resembles edema, but is termed "non-cardiogenic")
  5. Damage to Type II pneumocytes → impaired surfactant production, compounding the problem
  6. Formation of hyaline membranes (layered protein on the alveolar septa) — the pathologist's term for this overall picture is diffuse alveolar damage
  7. TGF-β and PDGF stimulate fibroblasts → recovery is possible, but the lung can also become organized/scarred
Why hyaline membranes impair oxygenation — A layer of protein coating the alveolar septum is a physical barrier between alveolar air and the capillary blood, making it very difficult for oxygen to reach hemoglobin — directly explaining the hypoxemia.
Acute interstitial pneumonia = ARDS with no known cause — If a patient meets the clinical/pathologic picture of ARDS but no inciting cause can be identified, the diagnosis becomes acute interstitial pneumonia (also called Hamman-Rich syndrome) — same process, different label based purely on whether an etiology is found.

Causes of ARDS

InfectionSepsis is a huge cause; diffuse pulmonary infections (viral — e.g., COVID-19 caused dramatic hyaline membrane formation at autopsy)
Physical injuryMechanical trauma, head injury (commonly associated), pulmonary contusion, near-drowning, fractures with fat embolism, burns, ionizing radiation
Inhaled irritantsHigh-concentration oxygen (even something we normally breathe can injure at high levels), smoke, irritant gases/chemicals (e.g., chlorine gas — described from an actual train-wreck exposure case)
Drug/chemical injuryHeroin or methadone overdose (survivors often develop bronchopneumonia), aspirin, barbiturate overdose, paraquat
Hematologic/otherTransfusion reactions, pancreatitis, uremia, cardiopulmonary bypass, hypersensitivity reactions
ARDS — gross
This lung was diffusely, palpably firm throughout — a finding that (as with many gross pathology findings) is sometimes best appreciated by feel rather than sight alone, reflecting the widespread hyaline membrane formation and consolidation.
Hyaline membranes — the classic ARDS finding
Layered pink (eosinophilic) protein coating the alveolar septa — a genuinely classic, must-know histologic finding. This same picture is seen in neonatal hyaline membrane disease, reflecting a broadly similar downstream mechanism (loss of effective surfactant function) despite different root causes.
ARDS — healing/organizing phase
In a patient who survived for a period of time, the alveolar septa show thickening, early fibrosis, and inflammatory infiltration as the body attempts to repair the damage — a possible substrate for later pulmonary hypertension if extensive enough, since the fibrotic septa also compromise the blood vessels running through them.

USMLE-Style Question

Which single cell type is considered most responsible for propagating the tissue damage seen in ARDS, through release of proteases and reactive oxygen species?

A. Alveolar macrophages
B. Eosinophils
C. Neutrophils
D. Type II pneumocytes
E. Lymphocytes
Answer: C. Neutrophils are the most important cell type in ARDS pathogenesis — once endothelial activation promotes their adhesion and recruitment, they release proteases and reactive oxygen species that substantially amplify the alveolar-capillary membrane damage.

6. Part 1 Lecture Cases

The four vignette questions Dr. Kemp used to open this part of the lecture.

Lecture Case 1

A 41-year-old male is stabbed in the chest. About 30 minutes later he develops shortness of breath and then collapses, becoming unresponsive. He cannot be resuscitated. At autopsy, 2 liters of blood are found in the left pleural cavity. The left lung is contracted, with a wrinkled pleural surface and dark, firm parenchyma, compared to the normal-appearing right lung. Which process explains these findings?

A. Compressive atelectasis
B. Resorptive atelectasis
C. Contraction atelectasis
D. Acute bronchopneumonia
E. Undiagnosed adenocarcinoma of the lung
Answer: A. This is compressive atelectasis from a hemothorax: the normally smooth pleural surface becomes wrinkled as the lung collapses under the pressure of the accumulated blood, and the parenchyma becomes firm as it is compressed together. There is no history suggesting an airway obstruction (resorptive) or chronic scarring process (contraction), and no time for a bronchopneumonia or occult malignancy to explain this acute presentation.

Lecture Case 2

A 38-year-old chronic alcoholic is found minimally responsive. He is found to have acute pancreatitis with markedly elevated amylase and lipase. Blood gases reveal hypoxemia and hypercapnia; he is intubated. Despite ventilator support, his condition worsens, and chest X-ray reveals diffuse infiltrates. Which cell type is most responsible for his pulmonary pathology?

A. Eosinophils
B. Alveolar macrophages
C. Type I pneumocytes
D. Neutrophils
E. Lymphocytes
Answer: D. Acute pancreatitis is a classic cause of ARDS. Neutrophils are the key cell type driving the alveolar-capillary damage and hyaline membrane formation that impairs oxygen transfer, explaining both the hypoxemia and the diffuse bilateral infiltrates on imaging, and the poor response to ventilator support.

Lecture Case 3

Two days after an open cholecystectomy with no complications, a 51-year-old non-smoker male with treated hypertension develops shortness of breath and decreased oxygen saturation. Chest X-ray reveals consolidation of the right lower lobe with no other changes. Vital signs are unremarkable aside from mild tachycardia and tachypnea. What is the most likely cause of these findings?

A. Undiagnosed neoplasm obstructing the airway
B. Hematoma formation from the surgery
C. Mucous plug of the airway
D. Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection
E. Aluminum-related pneumoconiosis
Answer: C. This is a classic postoperative resorptive atelectasis scenario: intubation/surgery predisposes to mucus plugging of an airway, causing localized lobar collapse. There is no risk factor for occult neoplasm, TB, or an occupational pneumoconiosis in this history, and a surgical hematoma would not explain isolated lower lobe consolidation on this timeline.

Lecture Case 4

A 53-year-old male is involved in a motor vehicle accident with multiple fractures and pulmonary contusions. His past medical history includes hypertension, diabetes, and a prior non-STEMI. Two days after admission he develops rapidly worsening hypoxia despite intubation and mechanical ventilation, and dies. At autopsy, the lung shows the finding below. What is the immediate cause of death?

Autopsy lung finding
Hyaline membranes lining the alveolar septa — no clear airspaces are visible, and there is no evidence of an obstructing airway lesion, thromboembolism, or pneumothorax in this field.
A. Pulmonary thromboembolism
B. Airway obstruction by an aspirated foreign body
C. Delayed tension pneumothorax
D. Acute respiratory distress syndrome
E. Undiagnosed pulmonary neoplasm
Answer: D. Multiple trauma with pulmonary contusion is a classic ARDS precipitant, and the histology (hyaline membranes, no visible airspaces) confirms diffuse alveolar damage. There is no vessel finding suggesting thromboembolism, no obstructing lesion, no neoplasm, and no pneumothorax-related finding in this image.

Part 2 Objectives

  1. List the types of obstructive lung disease and describe the general findings of pulmonary function testing for obstructive lung disease
  2. Compare and contrast chronic bronchitis and emphysema, including various types of emphysema, discussing risk factors, mechanism, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes
  3. Describe findings associated with α-1-antitrypsin disease
  4. Describe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
PART 2 — Chronic Bronchitis, Emphysema & COPD

7. Obstructive Lung Disease Overview

Forms: chronic bronchitis and emphysema (together = COPD), bronchiectasis, asthma, and small-airway disease (bronchiolitis) — the last three are covered in Part 3.

FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.7 defines obstructive lung disease
Why the ratio is low — reasoned, not memorized — Patients with obstructive disease can generally fill their lungs normally (so FVC is roughly preserved), but because the disease is obstructive, they can't empty their lungs well (so FEV1 is reduced) — hence a low ratio. Contrast this with restrictive lung disease, where both FEV1 and FVC are reduced roughly proportionally (from scarring), keeping the ratio close to normal.

8. Chronic Bronchitis

FeatureDetail
DescriptionClinical diagnosis: productive cough for 3+ months in 2+ consecutive years
EtiologyTobacco smoke (the vast majority of cases); also grain, cotton, or silica exposure
Clinical featuresHypercapnia, hypoxemia, cyanosis — "blue bloaters"
Same root cause as emphysema — Both chronic bronchitis and emphysema are most often driven by the same underlying risk factor (tobacco smoke), which is exactly why the two conditions so commonly coexist as combined COPD (Section 13) rather than presenting in isolation.

Pathogenesis

  • Goblet cell hyperplasia and hypertrophy → mucus hypersecretion — think of this as an exaggerated protective response: more mucus is the airway's attempt to shield itself from the inhaled irritant
  • Acute and chronic inflammatory infiltrates (damage to respiratory epithelium triggers an inflammatory response)
  • Tobacco smoke damages cilia, which normally clear the airway via the mucociliary escalator — impaired clearance means retained secretions
  • Infection can occur and acutely exacerbate the disease — all that stagnant, poorly-cleared mucus is an excellent growth substrate for bacteria
  • Smooth muscle hypertrophy and peribronchial fibrosis can develop, and can progress to obliterative bronchiolitis (obstruction of the bronchioles) — mucus and inflammation can track down from the bronchi into the smaller bronchioles rather than clearing up the escalator

Pathology

  • Hyperplasia/hypertrophy of the submucosal mucous glands
  • Reid index — ratio of mucous gland thickness to the thickness between the airway lumen and cartilage — is increased, directly reflecting the gland hyperplasia/hypertrophy

Complications

Cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure) — chronic scarring/obliterative bronchiolitis damages the alveolar septa and the blood vessels running through them, increasing pulmonary vascular resistance and straining the right heart over time.

USMLE-Style Question

A lung biopsy from a patient with a chronic productive cough shows a markedly increased ratio of mucous gland thickness to the distance between the airway lumen and cartilage. What is this ratio called, and what does its elevation reflect?

A. Reid index; goblet cell/mucous gland hyperplasia and hypertrophy
B. FEV1/FVC ratio; airway obstruction
C. Charcot-Leyden index; eosinophilic inflammation
D. Curschmann index; mucous plugging
E. A-a gradient; impaired gas exchange
Answer: A. The Reid index is the ratio of mucous gland thickness to the thickness between the airway lumen and cartilage. It is elevated in chronic bronchitis, directly reflecting the hyperplasia and hypertrophy of the submucosal mucous glands driving the excess mucus production.

9. Emphysema

FeatureDetail
DescriptionIrreversible enlargement of airspaces — destruction of the alveolar wall without fibrosis

Forms (Distinguished by Distribution)

FormDistributionEtiologyMost Severe In
CentriacinarRespiratory bronchioles only (proximal acinus); spares distal alveoliSmokingUpper lobes
PanacinarRespiratory bronchioles AND distal alveoli (entire acinus)α-1-antitrypsin deficiencyLower lobes/bases
Paraseptal (distal)Along the pleural surface—Specifically associated with bulla formation
IrregularVariable, associated with scarringAdjacent fibrosis—
Why upper vs. lower lobe distribution differs — Centriacinar (smoking-related) emphysema is worst in the upper lobes, plausibly because inhaled smoke tends to concentrate there (smoke "rises," and/or ventilation-to-perfusion differences favor greater deposition superiorly). Panacinar (AAT-related) emphysema, by contrast, is worst in the lower lobes/bases — so finding emphysema concentrated in the lower lobes should make you think AAT deficiency rather than ordinary smoking-related disease.

Pathogenesis

  • Activation of inflammatory mediators: LTB4, IL-8, TNF
  • Protease-antiprotease imbalance — relatively increased protease activity (especially elastase, released by inflammatory cells recruited by smoking) relative to antiprotease activity. Note: in ordinary smoking-related emphysema, the imbalance is mainly driven by more protease (from inflammatory cell recruitment), not necessarily less antiprotease — that's the specific mechanism in AAT deficiency (Section 12).
  • Oxidative stress — Nrf2 normally protects the lung from oxidant damage; mice lacking Nrf2 are at increased risk of smoke-induced lung damage (a nice mechanistic link from animal models to human disease)
  • Infection can exacerbate the disease process, though less prominently than in chronic bronchitis

Mechanism of Obstruction — Loss of Elastic Recoil

The key concept to actually understand (not just memorize) — Emphysema patients can usually breathe in without much difficulty — filling the lungs isn't the problem. The problem is breathing out: the destroyed elastic tissue that normally holds the airways open during expiration is gone, so as the patient tries to exhale, the small airways collapse before all the air can get out. This traps air distally — which is precisely why this is an obstructive disease despite the pathology being destruction of tissue rather than a literal physical blockage.

Pathologic Features

Gross: enlarged airspaces. Microscopic: enlarged airspaces.

Emphysema — gross
Rather than looking like normal, fine-sponge lung tissue, emphysematous lung looks like a spiderweb — thin strands of residual tissue with markedly enlarged spaces between them, heavily marked with black anthracotic (smoking-related) pigment.
Emphysema — histology
Markedly enlarged alveolar spaces with thin, sparse, often fragmented septa — the loss of surface area for gas exchange is visually obvious at this magnification.
Diagnostic caution — Emphysema should not be diagnosed microscopically unless it has also been appreciated grossly; conversely, once it's been seen grossly, the microscopic correlate is small fragments of residual septal tissue amid enlarged spaces. Also worth remembering: functional and structural findings don't always match — some patients clinically diagnosed with COPD have grossly and microscopically normal-appearing lungs at autopsy, a reminder that structural pathology is not the whole story of a disease's functional impact.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with severe COPD has particularly marked emphysematous destruction concentrated in the lower lobes/bases of both lungs on imaging, atypical for the usual smoking-related distribution. Which underlying condition should be specifically considered?

A. Chronic bronchitis alone
B. α-1-antitrypsin deficiency
C. Centriacinar emphysema from heavy smoking
D. Bronchiectasis
E. Asthma
Answer: B. Panacinar emphysema, classically associated with α-1-antitrypsin deficiency, is most severe in the lower lobes/bases — the opposite distribution from ordinary smoking-related centriacinar emphysema, which predominates in the upper lobes. A lower-lobe-predominant pattern should prompt consideration of AAT deficiency.

10. Other Forms of Emphysema

Compensatory hyperinflationAlveoli enlarge simply because it's mechanically necessary (e.g., adjacent lung has been removed or is non-functional) — not true emphysema in the destructive sense
Bullous emphysemaForms bullae — thin-walled air sacs on the pleural surface; classically in young males, not necessarily smokers; can rupture and cause a spontaneous pneumothorax
Interstitial emphysemaOccurs when air escapes into the soft tissue — classically after CPR with rib fractures, allowing breathed-in air to track into the subcutaneous soft tissue. Not a true disease process — a mechanical consequence of the rib fractures. At autopsy this can be felt as a distinctive "sponginess" when palpating the chest or extremities.
Bullous emphysema
Multiple thin-walled, cyst-like structures (bullae) on the pleural surface — these can occur singly or in clusters, as seen here. Rupture of a bulla is a recognized mechanism of spontaneous pneumothorax, especially in young males.

USMLE-Style Question

A previously healthy 22-year-old tall, thin male develops sudden-onset unilateral chest pain and dyspnea while playing basketball. Chest X-ray reveals a pneumothorax. Which underlying finding most likely predisposed him to this event?

A. Centriacinar emphysema from smoking
B. Rupture of a subpleural bulla
C. α-1-antitrypsin deficiency with panacinar emphysema
D. Interstitial emphysema from rib fracture
E. Compensatory hyperinflation
Answer: B. Spontaneous rupture of a subpleural bulla (bullous/paraseptal emphysema) is the classic cause of spontaneous pneumothorax in young, otherwise healthy males — not necessarily smokers, and not requiring any other underlying lung disease.

11. Emphysema vs. Chronic Bronchitis

FeatureEmphysemaChronic Bronchitis
Age50–75 years40–45 years
DyspneaSevere; earlier in courseMild; later in course
CoughLittle sputumMuch sputum
InfectionsUncommonCommon
Cor pulmonaleRareCommon
Airway resistanceNormal to slightly increasedIncreased
Elastic recoilDecreasedNormal
Reason through the table instead of memorizing it — Everything follows from the underlying mechanism. Chronic bronchitis = excess mucus (goblet cell hyperplasia) → productive sputum, a great medium for infection, and airway narrowing from secretions/inflammation (↑ resistance). Emphysema = tissue destruction with loss of elastic recoil → little sputum to produce, less of a nidus for infection, and the obstruction comes from dynamic airway collapse rather than intrinsic narrowing (so resistance is closer to normal, but recoil is what's lost).
Classic bedside descriptors — Emphysema patients are often called "pink puffers": they maintain oxygenation reasonably well but breathe rapidly/with effort (leaning forward, pursed-lip breathing). Chronic bronchitis patients are often called "blue bloaters": more cyanotic, with fluid retention from cor pulmonale.

12. Alpha-1-Antitrypsin Deficiency

α-1-antitrypsin is an anti-protease. When it's deficient, unchecked protease activity (especially elastase) damages lung tissue, producing emphysema — the mirror image of the "too much protease" mechanism seen in ordinary smoking-related emphysema, except here it's "too little antiprotease."

Pulmonary emphysemaPanacinar, lower lobe-predominant (Section 9)
Cirrhosisα-1-antitrypsin is produced in the liver; in AAT deficiency, misfolded protein doesn't export properly and accumulates within hepatocytes
GeneticsMost commonly associated with the PiZZ variant/genotype
Two organs, two different problems from the same defect — If the abnormal protein doesn't get out of the liver properly, it accumulates there and can cause cirrhosis. Whether or not it gets out, the protein still doesn't function correctly as an antiprotease — so pulmonary emphysema occurs either way.
α-1-antitrypsin deficiency — liver
Numerous small, round, eosinophilic (pink) globules within hepatocyte cytoplasm — these represent the misfolded, retained α-1-antitrypsin protein that failed to be properly secreted from the liver. Special stains (PAS with diastase) are typically used to highlight these more definitively in practice, but they can be appreciated on routine H&E as well, as shown here.

USMLE-Style Question

A 38-year-old non-smoker presents with dyspnea. CT shows panacinar emphysema most severe at the lung bases. Liver biopsy performed for unrelated elevated liver enzymes shows numerous round eosinophilic globules within hepatocytes. Which genetic variant is most commonly associated with this presentation?

A. PiMM (normal)
B. ΔF508
C. TSC2 loss-of-function
D. PiZZ
E. HFE C282Y
Answer: D. This presentation — panacinar, base-predominant emphysema in a non-smoker plus hepatocellular globules representing misfolded, retained protein — is classic for α-1-antitrypsin deficiency, most commonly associated with the PiZZ genotype.

13. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)

Description: combined features of emphysema and chronic bronchitis.

Why the two so often travel together — Since both emphysema and chronic bronchitis are most commonly caused by the same risk factor (smoking), patients most often have some component of both processes, even though each has genuinely distinct pathology and mechanism when considered separately (Section 11). In practice, medical records and autopsy diagnoses far more often say simply "COPD" rather than cleanly separating out "emphysema" vs. "chronic bronchitis" individually.
Point to ponder — in which patient would you see pure emphysema WITHOUT a chronic bronchitis component? α-1-antitrypsin deficiency in a non-smoker. Since AAT deficiency causes emphysema through a completely separate mechanism (antiprotease deficiency, not smoking-related epithelial/goblet cell damage), a non-smoking AAT-deficient patient can have pure emphysema without any chronic bronchitis component — they simply never had the smoking-driven insult that produces goblet cell hyperplasia and hypersecretion in the first place. (If that same patient also smokes, they're now at risk for a chronic bronchitis component too.)

14. Part 2 Summary Table

TopicKey Fact
Obstructive lung disease definitionFEV1/FVC < 0.7 (can fill lungs, can't empty them)
Chronic bronchitis definitionProductive cough ≥3 months, ≥2 consecutive years (clinical diagnosis)
Chronic bronchitis mechanismGoblet cell hyperplasia/hypertrophy, ciliary damage, inflammation
Reid index↑ mucous gland thickness : lumen-to-cartilage thickness ratio
Chronic bronchitis complicationCor pulmonale
Centriacinar emphysemaSmoking; respiratory bronchioles only; upper lobes
Panacinar emphysemaAAT deficiency; entire acinus; lower lobes/bases
Paraseptal (distal) emphysemaPleural surface; forms bullae
Emphysema pathogenesisLTB4/IL-8/TNF activation; protease-antiprotease imbalance (elastase↑); oxidative stress (Nrf2 protective); infection can exacerbate
Emphysema mechanism of obstructionLoss of elastic recoil → airway collapse on exhalation → air trapping
Bullous emphysemaYoung males; rupture → spontaneous pneumothorax
Interstitial emphysemaAir in soft tissue after CPR/rib fractures — mechanical, not a disease process
Emphysema vs. bronchitisOlder/severe early dyspnea/little sputum/uncommon infection/rare cor pulmonale vs. Younger/mild late dyspnea/much sputum/common infection/common cor pulmonale
Pink puffers vs. blue bloatersEmphysema vs. chronic bronchitis

15. Part 2 Lecture Case

Lecture Case

A 69-year-old female with a 60 pack-year smoking history reports several years of increasing shortness of breath. In clinic, she is leaning forward with an increased respiratory rate; her fingernails are not cyanotic. She has a cough that is not frequently productive. What is the most likely mechanism underlying her disease process?

A. Overproduction of elastase relative to antiprotease activity
B. Goblet cell hyperplasia with mucus hypersecretion
C. Diminished α-1-antitrypsin production
D. Mast cell activation with bronchoconstriction
E. Loss-of-function mutation in TSC2
Answer: A. This is the classic emphysema ("pink puffer") presentation: an older patient with a heavy smoking history, severe early dyspnea, tachypnea with a forward-leaning posture, non-cyanotic nail beds, and a non-productive cough. The mechanism is a protease-antiprotease imbalance driven by smoking-induced inflammatory cell recruitment and elastase release — not a primary antiprotease deficiency (she has a heavy smoking history, making AAT deficiency less likely as the primary driver), and not a bronchoconstrictive or allergic process.

Part 3 Objectives

  1. Describe bronchiectasis and asthma, including various types of asthma, discussing risk factors, mechanism, symptoms, and pathologic changes
  2. Describe pathogenesis and clinical manifestations of cystic fibrosis, and describe the mechanism and its relation to the sweat chloride test
PART 3 — Asthma, Bronchiectasis & Cystic Fibrosis

16. Asthma

FeatureDetail
DescriptionEpisodic bronchoconstriction due to hyper-reactive airways
FormsAtopic (allergen sensitization) or non-atopic (no allergen sensitization) — drug-induced and occupational asthma are sometimes listed as separate categories, but conceptually fall under one or the other
TriggersSeasonal, exercise, drugs (e.g., aspirin), occupational exposures, and smoking ("asthmatic bronchitis")
Clinical presentationWheezing, cough, shortness of breath

Atopic vs. Non-Atopic Asthma

AtopicNon-Atopic
Family historyCommon (often with rhinitis, urticaria, or eczema — other allergic-origin conditions)Less common
TriggersEnvironmental allergens (dust, animal dander), foods, ± viral infectionViral illness, inhaled pollutants (e.g., sulfur dioxide), cold, exercise
Determining which type a patient has — There isn't an absolute test that instantly sorts every case; you look at the whole picture — family history, personal history of other allergic conditions, and allergy testing — rather than relying on any single trigger, since there's real overlap in triggers between the two categories.

Aspirin-induced asthma works through effects on prostaglandin synthesis, not a classic allergic mechanism. Occupational asthma is a reminder to always ask patients about their occupation and hobbies — exposure history is diagnostically important across many of the conditions in this unit, and the same substance (e.g., silica) can cause more than one distinct lung pathology depending on the individual's response.

Pathogenesis (Atopic Asthma)

  • IgE-mediated, TH2 cell activation — an over-response to inhaled antigen
  • TH2 cells produce IL-4 (stimulates IgE production) and IL-13 (stimulates both IgE production and mucin production)
  • IL-5 activates eosinophils — eosinophilic infiltration is a characteristic feature of both atopic and non-atopic asthma
  • Early phase: bronchoconstriction, mediated by histamine, prostaglandin D2, and leukotrienes C4/D4/E4
  • Late phase: eotaxin promotes recruitment of eosinophils and additional TH2 cells, sustaining/amplifying the inflammatory response

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with asthma is found to have prominent eosinophilic airway inflammation. Which interleukin is most directly responsible for recruiting and activating these eosinophils?

A. IL-4
B. IL-13
C. IL-5
D. IL-8
E. IL-2
Answer: C. IL-5 is the key cytokine responsible for eosinophil activation in asthma. (IL-4 stimulates IgE production; IL-13 stimulates both IgE and mucin production — distinct roles from IL-5's eosinophil-specific effect.)

17. Asthma Pathology

GrossHyperinflation; mucous plugging of airways (Curschmann spirals — spiral-shaped mucus plugs)
MicroscopicSmooth muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia; sub-basement membrane fibrosis (the basement membrane appears thickened); mucous gland hyperplasia/hypertrophy; eosinophilic infiltrate; Charcot-Leyden crystals
Charcot-Leyden crystals — needle/spindle-shaped crystals formed from crystallized eosinophil major basic protein. Know not just the buzzword but what it actually looks like under the microscope — exam questions sometimes describe the appearance rather than naming the buzzword directly, expecting you to recognize the morphology itself.

Status Asthmaticus

A severe, life-threatening asthma exacerbation: the patient can breathe in but progressively cannot breathe out — breathe in, can't breathe out, breathe in, can't breathe out — leading to severe hyperinflation. This is a real danger even in patients who manage their asthma carefully; good chronic control does not guarantee an acute episode can't become life-threatening.

Fatal status asthmaticus — gross
Markedly hyperinflated lungs, bulging outward against the ribs and nearly meeting at the midline within the chest cavity — the direct anatomic consequence of severe, sustained air trapping.
Airway with mucous plug — low power
An airway (cartilage visible at left) whose lumen is filled with a dense mucous plug, with inflammatory cells admixed. Note the inner airway wall surface has an undulating, wavy contour rather than a smooth one — a visual cue to underlying smooth muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia even before examining at higher power.
Smooth muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia with eosinophilic infiltrate
Thickened bands of submucosal smooth muscle with a dense underlying inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils — the cellular correlate of the airway hyper-reactivity driving bronchoconstriction in asthma.
Eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals — high power
Eosinophils are identifiable both by their bright red-pink (eosinophilic) cytoplasmic granules and their characteristic bilobed nuclei (visible at this magnification). The elongated, needle-shaped structures near the center are Charcot-Leyden crystals, formed from crystallized eosinophil major basic protein — this is exactly what the "buzzword" actually looks like under the scope.

USMLE-Style Question

Autopsy of a patient who died during a severe asthma exacerbation reveals markedly hyperinflated lungs and, on histology, spiral-shaped mucous plugs within the airways. What is the specific name for these spiral mucous plugs?

A. Charcot-Leyden crystals
B. Ferruginous bodies
C. Mallory-Denk bodies
D. Curschmann spirals
E. Psammoma bodies
Answer: D. Curschmann spirals are the spiral-shaped mucous plugs classically found in the airways in asthma (and status asthmaticus), reflecting mucus that has taken on the shape of the small airways it plugged.

18. Bronchiectasis

FeatureDetail
DescriptionPermanent dilation of bronchi and bronchioles due to loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue, secondary to necrotizing infection
CausesCongenital/hereditary: cystic fibrosis, intralobar sequestration, Kartagener syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia). Infectious: a single severe infection or recurrent infections. Bronchial obstruction (e.g., tumor).
MechanismObstruction AND infection — the two are interrelated: obstruction predisposes to downstream infection, and infection/inflammation can itself contribute to further obstruction
Clinical presentationSevere cough with production of fetid (foul-smelling) sputum; dyspnea; hemoptysis
ComplicationsHypoxia, hypercapnia, pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale; amyloidosis (from sustained chronic inflammation)
Why the sputum is so foul-smelling — Chronically infected, poorly-cleared secretions sit trapped in dilated, damaged airways — essentially stagnant material that gets coughed up, explaining both the volume and the fetid odor.
Why cilia matter — Kartagener syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia) impairs the cilia that normally clear the airways. Losing that clearance mechanism sets up the same obstruction + infection cycle that drives bronchiectasis from any other cause.

Pathology

GrossEnlarged/dilated airways, traceable out to (or very near) the pleural surface — normally, airways can only be traced out to within a couple of centimeters of the pleural surface
MicroscopicFibrosis, acute and chronic inflammation (a chronic process, so both acute and chronic changes can be seen simultaneously)
Permanent vs. temporary dilation — Airway dilation can occur temporarily in other settings, but by definition, bronchiectasis is permanent — that distinction is part of what makes the diagnosis, not just the presence of dilation itself.
Bronchiectasis — gross
Forceps trace a dilated airway (cartilage visible within its wall) extending abnormally far out toward the pleural surface — well beyond where a normal bronchus/bronchiole would be traceable.

USMLE-Style Question

Which of the following complications of long-standing bronchiectasis results from sustained chronic inflammation and abnormal protein deposition, rather than directly from hypoxia or pulmonary vascular changes?

A. Cor pulmonale
B. Pulmonary hypertension
C. Amyloidosis
D. Hypercapnia
E. Digital clubbing
Answer: C. Amyloidosis (secondary/AA type) can develop as a complication of any sustained chronic inflammatory state, including long-standing bronchiectasis, from persistently elevated serum amyloid A protein — distinct from the hypoxia-driven complications like cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension, and hypercapnia.

19. Cystic Fibrosis & the Sweat Chloride Test

A helpful conceptual anchor: water follows sodium, and sodium and chloride tend to move together. So if you disrupt the chloride channel, you disrupt sodium handling, and therefore water handling too.

CFTR/ENaC Mechanism

Normal airway/pancreatic duct/intestineCFTR exports chloride into the lumen; CFTR normally inhibits the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC)
In CF (airway/pancreas/intestine)Loss of CFTR function → chloride excretion into the lumen is blocked → ENaC activity increases (loss of normal CFTR inhibition) → increased sodium (and secondary water) reabsorption out of the lumen → the luminal secretions are left dehydrated and abnormally viscous/tenacious
Normal sweat ductChloride is normally reabsorbed into the cell from the sweat duct lumen, and sodium follows it back into the body
In CF (sweat duct) — the exceptionCFTR loss means chloride cannot be reabsorbed from the duct lumen → sodium stays in the lumen too (can't follow the chloride back in) → sweat is left with high chloride (and sodium) content — this is the basis of the sweat chloride test
The critical distinction to keep straight — In the airway/pancreas/intestine, CF causes excess sodium/water reabsorption out of the lumen (dehydrated secretions). In the sweat duct specifically, CF causes failure of sodium/chloride reabsorption back into the body (salty sweat). The direction of the defect's clinical consequence is opposite between these two settings, even though the root molecular defect (loss of CFTR chloride transport) is the same.

Complications by System

PancreaticPancreatic exocrine insufficiency
GI (neonatal)Meconium ileus
SinopulmonarySinusitis; pneumonia (classically Pseudomonas); bronchiectasis
Reproductive (males)Bilateral obstruction/absence of the vas deferens → infertility
HepatobiliaryBile stasis → cirrhosis
Bronchiectasis link — Cystic fibrosis is one of the classic congenital/hereditary causes of bronchiectasis (Section 18): the thick, dehydrated mucus sets up exactly the obstruction + chronic infection cycle that drives permanent airway dilation.

USMLE-Style Question

In a patient with cystic fibrosis, which of the following correctly describes the direction of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) defect in the sweat duct compared to the airway epithelium?

A. ENaC activity increases in both the sweat duct and the airway
B. ENaC activity decreases in both the sweat duct and the airway
C. ENaC activity decreases in the airway but increases in the sweat duct
D. ENaC is not expressed in either tissue
E. ENaC activity increases in the airway (dehydrated secretions) but decreases in the sweat duct (salty sweat)
Answer: E. In the airway (and pancreas/intestine), loss of CFTR removes its normal inhibition of ENaC, so ENaC activity increases, driving excess sodium/water reabsorption and dehydrated secretions. In the sweat duct, the situation is reversed — the clinically relevant defect there is failure of chloride (and secondarily sodium) reabsorption back into the body, leaving sweat abnormally salty — the basis of the sweat chloride test.

21. Part 3 Lecture Cases

Lecture Case 1

A 23-year-old male is brought to the ED with an hour of severe shortness of breath, prominent wheezing, and cough. His usual therapy has been ineffective. He has no other past medical history, but his father has the same disease process. With treatment, he recovers. Which mediator was most likely responsible for this acute episode?

A. Cyclooxygenase-2
B. Tumor necrosis factor-alpha alone
C. Complement C5a
D. Rheumatoid factor
E. IgE
Answer: E. The family history strongly suggests atopic asthma, an IgE-mediated process, presenting classically with wheezing, cough, and shortness of breath. The other options are not the primary drivers of an atopic asthma exacerbation.

Lecture Case 2

A 53-year-old non-smoking female with influenza A develops shaking chills, fever, productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain. Chest X-ray shows consolidation of the lower left and right upper lobes; sputum culture grows Staphylococcus aureus. Despite treatment, she doesn't fully resolve, and is hospitalized. About one week after discharge, she develops a cough productive of foul-smelling, green-yellow, creamy sputum. What would radiologic or pathologic examination of the lungs most likely reveal at this point?

A. Loss of pulmonary parenchyma consistent with emphysema
B. Numerous air-filled sacs on the pleural surface
C. Numerous 1-2 cm nodules throughout the lungs
D. Air in the pleural space
E. Dilation of the airways
Answer: E. This sequence — severe necrotizing pneumonia (influenza with secondary S. aureus superinfection) followed by foul-smelling, purulent sputum — describes the development of bronchiectasis, with dilation of the damaged, chronically infected airways. She is a non-smoker (making emphysema unlikely), and there is nothing in the history suggesting bullae/pneumothorax or a metastatic/neoplastic process to explain multiple nodules.

Lecture Case 3

A 22-year-old male is admitted for shortness of breath with a severe cough producing fetid mucopurulent sputum, with several similar prior episodes. Pulmonary function testing shows a low FEV1/FVC ratio, and sweat chloride testing is within normal limits. He and his wife have been unable to conceive despite attempts. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Cystic fibrosis
B. Chronic bronchitis from smoking
C. α-1-antitrypsin deficiency
D. Idiopathic bronchiectasis with no identifiable cause
E. Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome)
Answer: E. This presentation (recurrent bronchiectasis-type symptoms plus infertility) could initially suggest cystic fibrosis — which can also cause infertility via vas deferens abnormalities — but a normal sweat chloride test argues against CF. Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) causes the same obstruction/infection cycle from impaired ciliary clearance, and is also associated with infertility (impaired sperm motility, among other ciliary dysfunction effects), fitting this picture with a normal sweat chloride result.

22. Master High-Yield Pearls (All Three Parts)

  • Atelectasis direction logic: resorptive/obstruction → collapse from within (nothing refills); compressive → collapse from without (something pushes in); contraction → collapse that can't fill in the first place (scarring). All three follow directly from their mechanism, not rote memorization.
  • Pulmonary edema = "hemodynamic," not just "cardiogenic" — several causes (hypoalbuminemia, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome) have nothing to do with the heart.
  • ARDS is non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, driven by neutrophil-mediated alveolar-capillary injury → hyaline membranes → diffuse alveolar damage. Same histologic endpoint as neonatal hyaline membrane disease, different root cause (injury vs. developmental surfactant deficiency).
  • Obstructive lung disease = FEV1/FVC < 0.7 — can fill the lungs, can't empty them. Contrast with restrictive disease, where both values fall proportionally and the ratio stays roughly normal.
  • Chronic bronchitis = mucus/goblet cell problem (clinical diagnosis, productive cough). Emphysema = tissue destruction/elastic recoil problem (irreversible airspace enlargement, no fibrosis). Both usually coexist as COPD because they share the same root cause: smoking.
  • Emphysema distribution tells you the cause: upper lobes → smoking (centriacinar); lower lobes/bases → α-1-antitrypsin deficiency (panacinar).
  • Bullous (paraseptal) emphysema → young males → spontaneous pneumothorax from bulla rupture.
  • AAT deficiency = PiZZ genotype → emphysema (unchecked protease activity) + cirrhosis (misfolded protein retained in hepatocytes). The one setting where you can see pure emphysema without any chronic bronchitis component, if the patient doesn't smoke.
  • Asthma = episodic, reversible bronchoconstriction (vs. emphysema's irreversible airway collapse) — atopic (IgE/TH2, family history of allergy) vs. non-atopic (viral/irritant triggers, less family history), but both are eosinophil-rich processes with Charcot-Leyden crystals.
  • Bronchiectasis = permanent airway dilation from the linked cycle of obstruction + infection — caused by CF, PCD/Kartagener, severe/recurrent infection, or an obstructing lesion.
  • Cystic fibrosis — same CFTR defect, opposite functional consequence depending on tissue: dehydrated secretions everywhere ENaC activity goes up (airway, pancreas, gut) vs. salty sweat where the sweat duct fails to reabsorb chloride/sodium back into the body.
  • Recurring theme across all three parts: work out the pathophysiology from first principles (anatomy, the specific molecular/cellular defect) rather than memorizing disconnected fact lists — nearly every comparison table in this lecture set can be reconstructed this way.
